meta.topic: Composites: layup / cure tool life by tool material, layup deposition rates, volume-route cycle times and annual volumes, autoclave cycle and load norms
meta.for: docs/review/report-standard-2026-11/README.md §2 — the hat stiffener's 500-part tool life (37–39 % of the price), hand layup at ~6.5 kg/h, autoclave prepreg at 200k/yr
rules: Every figure below was read on the page or PDF named in `url`. Search-result snippets were NOT used as sources.
read_method 'pdf-text': the PDF was downloaded with plain curl and the quote is copied from pdftotext output (exact text).

read_method 'webfetch': the page was opened with the WebFetch tool, which returns the page through a summarising model; quotes are what that tool returned as verbatim and should be spot-checked against the live page before a quote is printed in a report.
Vendor / trade-press figures are labelled `kind: vendor-claim` or `trade-press`; none is a measured production statistic unless `kind` says so.
No user-agent spoofing or bot-check bypass. Pages that refused (403 / 429 / DNS / reset) are listed under `not_used` and were not used.

findings.conditions: epoxy tooling, cure temperature not exceeding 185 °C; Cytec statement
findings.source: Bruce Morey, 'Tooling It Up for Composites', SME Media (Manufacturing Engineering)
findings.quote: Epoxy tooling is generally limited to less than 300 cure cycles at temperatures not exceeding 185°C

findings.conditions: at 375 °F / 191 °C; supplier claim
findings.source: Bruce Morey, 'Tooling It Up for Composites', SME Media
findings.quote: (over 1000 cure cycles at 375°F or 191°C)

findings.toolMaterial: carbon/BMI composite layup tool (Hexcel HexTool M61)
findings.value: several hundred; > 500 part cure cycles demonstrated
findings.conditions: 180 °C (356 °F) cure carbon fibre tools
findings.source: Hexcel, HexTool M61 product data sheet (global), Copyright 2015
findings.quote: HexTool® has proved to be dimensionally stable with the ability to hold vacuum integrity before and after machining, and after more than 500 part cure cycles. ... Formulated to withstand several hundred autoclave cycles at 180°C (356°F)

findings.conditions: at 355 °F (180 °C); older M61 resin datasheet (©2015/2016) — Hexcel's newer HexTool sheet says 'several hundred'
findings.source: Hexcel, HexTool M61 / HexPly M61 data sheet
findings.quote: Proven M61 performance capable of 1000 tool thermal cycles at 355°F (180°C)

findings.conditions: CompositesWorld M&P reference page
findings.source: CW Editorial Team, 'Materials & Processes: Tooling for composites', CompositesWorld
findings.quote: has a CTE that matches carbon/epoxy parts and can survive 500 autoclave cycles

findings.toolMaterial: metal ('hard') tools incl. Invar; composite ('soft') tools
findings.value: metal: 'many thousands of production cycles'; composite: 'relatively low-volume production' (no number)
findings.conditions: general statement; Invar named as the most durable and most costly
findings.source: CW Editorial Team, 'Materials & Processes: Tooling for composites', CompositesWorld
findings.quote: metal tools, although relatively heavy and expensive, are able to withstand many thousands of production cycles. ... The most durable, but also most costly, are made of high-performance steel-and-nickel alloys, such as Invar. ... they are more vulnerable to wear, and they typically find service in relatively low-volume production

findings.value: life of the programme
findings.conditions: aerospace programme; no cycle count given
findings.source: Jim Lorincz, 'Tooling to Match Composite Production', SME Media
findings.quote: The durability of Invar reduced total cost of ownership, and tooling would last the life of the program.

findings.conditions: supplier statement (Weber Manufacturing); heat-up 66 °C/min claimed
findings.source: Bruce Morey, 'Tooling It Up for Composites', SME Media
findings.quote: They are very well suited for making 1000–100,000 parts or more,

findings.process: slush moulding of instrument-panel skins — context only
findings.value: 10,000 (geometric grain) / 85,000 (random grain)
findings.conditions: European manufacturers' reports; thermal cycling 110–475 °F every 3–4 min; not autoclave composites — use only as an order-of-magnitude for nickel shells under thermal cycling
findings.source: Morris Mengel, 'Lessons in the Use of Electroformed Nickel Tools', MoldMaking Technology
findings.quote: Some European manufacturers reported that geometric pattern tool life averages 10,000 parts per tool ... a tool life of 85,000 parts per tool with older animal grain (random grain) patterns

findings.unit: parts per die set ('as many as')
findings.conditions: glass SMC; CW process overview
findings.source: CW Editorial Team, 'High-volume molding methods', CompositesWorld
findings.quote: As many as 200,000 parts can be turned out on a set of forged steel dies

findings.toolMaterial: steel SMC tool; open mould; RTM tool
findings.conditions: 1998 article by an RTM tooling company; life depends on the finish required (Class A shorter)
findings.source: John Moore (JHM Technologies), 'Demystifying the RTM Process'
findings.quote: Tool Life* >100,000 >1,000 >1,000 to 5,000 ... Expected tooling life for a steel tool as used in the SMC process is greater then 100,000 moldings.

findings.toolMaterial: steel (AISI 4140 pre-hardened 30–32 HRC), nickel or chrome plated
findings.value: AISI 4140, 30–32 HRC, plated
findings.conditions: CKN Knowledge in Practice Centre page A302 (draft, last edited 2022-07-26)
findings.source: Composites Knowledge Network (CKN), 'Compression moulding - A302'
findings.quote: are usually made of steel and are nickel or chrome plated ... AISI 4140 alloy steel or equivalent pre-hardened to Rockwell C hardness of 30-32

findings.conditions: flat laminate charge of 4–40 plies, carbon/epoxy prepreg; customer baseline in a tape-head trial
findings.source: Sara Black, 'New Equipment Brings Tape Placement Within Reach Of Smaller Shops', CompositesWorld
findings.quote: take several hours to produce, at an average throughput speed of about 2 lb/hr

findings.conditions: 3-inch carbon/epoxy tape, flat tabletop tool, 20 in/s average, ply drop-offs included; same trial as LR-1
findings.source: Sara Black, CompositesWorld (as LR-1)
findings.quote: layed material at an average rate of 20 lb/hr at an average speed of 20 ips

findings.value: hand: 'a few pounds' per hour; AFP: > 100 lb (45+ kg) per hour
findings.conditions: AFP figure 'depending on part geometry'; knowledge-centre page, undated, sponsored
findings.source: CompositesWorld Automated Composites Knowledge Center, 'Manufacturing Processes'
findings.quote: While traditional hand layup methods can deposit a few pounds of material per hour, ... AFP can deposit over 100 pounds (45+ kg) per hour at a rate of over 3,000 inches per minute

findings.value: 787 projected ~50, achieved ~1/5 of that (~10); today large production systems 100; very large > 200
findings.conditions: aircraft-scale parts (fuselage / wing skins), not small automotive parts
findings.source: Bjorn Fehrm, 'Bjorn's Corner: Aircraft Structures Part 15. Automated layup systems', Leeham News
findings.quote: it was projected that a system could lay down around 50kg tape per hour. ... In reality, it was one-fifth of that rate ... Today, a large production-oriented system can achieve 100kg/hour. ... very large, fast systems lay down over 200kg/hour.

findings.value: hand 2–3; AFP 10–150 (also 30–75 in another table on the same page)
findings.conditions: AFP machine vendor blog; no citation for the figures; internally inconsistent — CONTEXT ONLY, do not use as a basis
findings.source: Addcomposites, 'AFP vs Hand Layup: The Manufacturing Revolution Reshaping Composite Production'
findings.quote: Production Speed ... 2-3 kg/hour ... 10-150 kg/hour

findings.system: Hexcel HexPly M21 (180 °C aerospace toughened epoxy), monolithic part < 15 mm
findings.value: heat RT→180 °C at 1–2 °C/min; hold 120 ± 5 min; cool at 2–5 °C/min; vent at ≤ 60 °C; 7 bar
findings.conditions: derived total (this research, arithmetic): heat 160 K ÷ 1–2 K/min = 80–160 min + 120 min + cool 120 K ÷ 2–5 K/min = 24–60 min ⇒ 224–340 min = 3.7–5.7 h, excluding pressurise / load / unload / thermocouple set-up
findings.source: Hexcel, HexPly M21 product data sheet, Copyright 2020
findings.quote: 4. Set heat-up rate from room temperature to 180°C ±5°C (356°F ±9°F) to achieve an actual component heat-up rate between 1-2°C/minute (2-4°F/ minute). 5. Hold at 180°C ±5°C (356°F ±9°F) for 120 minutes ±5 minutes. 6. Cool component at an actual cooldown rate of 2-5°C/minute (4-9°F/minute). 7. Vent autoclave pressure when the component reaches 60°C (140°F) or below.

findings.system: Hexcel HexPly M77 fast-cure epoxy prepreg (automotive / sports goods)
findings.value: 10 min to 140 °C + 7 min dwell + 6 min cool-down = 23 min; 7 bar
findings.conditions: 'strongly dependent on the part geometry, thickness and capability of the autoclave'; the guide adds that autoclaves need longer cycles than compression moulding because of the autoclave's thermal mass
findings.source: Hexcel, HexPly M77 User Guide, ©2016
findings.quote: Time to T. 10 min. Temperature 140 °C Dwell 7 min. Pressure 7 bar Time to cool down 6 min. ... Longer cure cycles (compared to compression molding) are required due to fact that the large autoclave mass takes a long time to heat up and cool down.

findings.system: carbon/epoxy prepreg, automotive (Plasan / Globe RapidClave context); aerospace benchmark
findings.value: autoclave 'almost 2 hours' v RapidClave 17 min (Gen 1), 6–8 min (Gen 2); aerospace: 8 h 'considered fast'
findings.conditions: Corvette Stingray parts; the 8-h figure is the interviewee's statement about large aerospace parts
findings.source: Peggy Malnati, 'Sub-8-minute cycle times on carbon/epoxy prepreg', CompositesWorld
findings.quote: from almost 2 hours in an autoclave to a mere 17 minutes ... a cycle time much shorter than the 8 hours he says is currently considered fast in the aerospace industry

findings.system: University of Washington ME composites shop autoclave
findings.value: 100 in long, 35.38 in bed width, 42.75 in tube diameter, 10–89 psi, 400 °F; heat ≤ 10 °F/min, cool ≤ 3 °F/min
findings.conditions: a small (≈ 2.5 × 0.9 m bed) autoclave — the same class as CostVision's '1200 mm autoclave' bed of 2.8 × 1.0 m; equipment ramp limits, not part ramp rates
findings.source: University of Washington Mechanical Engineering, Composites shop page
findings.quote: The length of the autoclave is 100 inches, and the width of the bed is 35.38 inches ... 10 °F per minute max. heating rate ... 3 °F per minute max. cooling rate

findings.conditions: maker's reference list; no heating / cooling rates or cycle times published on the page
findings.source: Maschinenbau Scholz, 'Hot-air autoclaves for composite'
findings.quote: Feeding diameter: 500 mm - 9.000 mm ... Feeding length: 500 mm - 50.000 mm ... Pressure: 0 - 70 bar

findings.process: prepreg compression moulding (PCM) — Mitsubishi Rayon, Nissan GT-R decklid (MY2014)
findings.value: press 8 min at 140 °C, 8 MPa; preforming < 5 min (1 min heat to 60–70 °C, 0.3 MPa); 84,000 parts/yr/tool (3-min-cure prepreg), 50,000 parts/yr/tool (5-min-cure)
findings.conditions: first commercial PCM; 'reportedly'; preform tool polyurethane board; mould tool material not stated
findings.source: Peggy Malnati, 'Prepreg compression molding makes its commercial debut', CompositesWorld
findings.quote: The molding cycle in a hydraulic compression press is 8 minutes at 140°C, using 8 MPa forming pressure. ... The PCM process reportedly can produce 84,000 parts per year per tool, using the 3-minute-cure prepreg and 50,000 per year per tool, using the 5-minute-cure prepreg.

findings.process: press cure of fast-cure prepreg (Hexcel HexPly M77)
findings.value: isothermal cure 2 min at 150 °C (3 min at 140, 5 min at 130, 7 min at 120); 'designed for hot-in/hot-out compression molding'; 130 °C / 5 min recommended for compression
findings.conditions: cure only — loading, closing, demould and preforming are additional
findings.source: Hexcel, HexPly M77 User Guide, ©2016
findings.quote: Extra fast cure in 2 min @150°C (302°F) ... Designed for hot-in/ hot-out compression molding ... For compression molding, a less aggressive cure cycle is recommended (130°C/5min).

findings.value: aerospace EP2750: takt ≤ 30 min ⇒ 10,000 parts/yr/tool; automotive prepregs: takt ≤ 3 min for small-medium parts; matched metal tools, steel mould
findings.conditions: Solvay Heanor automated line
findings.source: Ginger Gardiner, 'Novel prepreg for compression molding in RAPM', CompositesWorld
findings.quote: This takt time of 30 minutes or less enables an annual production volume of 10,000 parts per tool. ... takt times of 3 minutes or less for small to medium parts using automotive prepregs

findings.value: 14,000–40,000 parts = very high volume for CFRP prepreg; 20,000–25,000/yr on one line (Corvette roof) = prepreg's sweet spot; automotive high volume starts ~100,000; suppliers target 80,000–100,000/yr with 2–3 min compression cycles; compression moulding cuts 'as much as four hours' to 5–10 min
findings.conditions: Huntsman (Adam Harms) and other supplier statements
findings.source: ACMA / Composites Manufacturing magazine, 'Fast-cure Prepreg is Making Inroads'
findings.quote: About 14,000 to 40,000 parts would be considered very high volume for CFRP prepreg ... Around 20,000 to 25,000 parts per year on a single production line such as the Corvette roof ... In automotive, you haven't reached high volume until about 100,000 parts. ... qualifying prepreg for high-volume production in the area of 80,000 to 100,000 parts per year.

findings.value: realistic 3–7 min per part; BMW i3/i8 cure < 10 min; low-pressure RTM 30–60 min; volumes moved from 1,000–4,000 to 12,000–50,000 parts/yr; preforming slower than the mould cycle
findings.conditions: KraussMaffei (Erich Fries), Engel (Matthias Mayr), Mubea Carbo Tech statements
findings.source: Ginger Gardiner, 'The rise of HP-RTM', CompositesWorld
findings.quote: parts are realistically produced in 3 to 7 minutes, a function of part size and complexity. ... BMW reports that its cure cycle for i3 and i8 parts is less than 10 minutes ... But now, with 12,000 to 50,000 parts per year ... The cutting, positioning and forming of fabric layers takes longer than the mold cycle.

findings.value: 50,000–80,000 parts per line per year needs ≤ 3 min; only 1-min cure + 10 s injection + 6 s compression reached 166 s
findings.unit: cycle / parts per line per year
findings.conditions: nine-stage cycle: load preform, close, vacuum, inject, compress, cure, open, demould, clean
findings.source: Michael LeGault, 'Fraunhofer ICT in-mold pressure sensors for HP-RTM', CompositesWorld
findings.quote: Producing 50,000-80,000 parts per line per year requires a cycle time of 3 minutes or less.

findings.value: up to 30,000 vehicles per year (first serial HP-RTM, 2013)
findings.conditions: KraussMaffei webinar description
findings.source: Gardner Business Media event page, 'HP-RTM in Automotive and Aviation Applications' (KraussMaffei, S. Schmidhuber)
findings.quote: In 2013, the first HP-RTM systems went into automotive serial production, making parts for up to 30,000 vehicles per year.

findings.value: Dieffenbacher ~180 s; Dow < 60 s total; Hexion 75–135 s; Huntsman DFCM ~1.30 min; paper example: 294 parts/day (> 73,000 parts/yr), 4 workers + 1 foreman per line, part €70 (material €49); BMW 7 Series side sills / tunnel / roof bows
findings.conditions: supplier claims; WCM suits less complex geometry than HP-RTM
findings.source: Ginger Gardiner, 'Wet compression molding', CompositesWorld
findings.quote: Dieffenbacher reports molding cycles cut to ~180 seconds ... The paper calculates a part cost of 70€, raw material cost of 49 €, daily production rate of 294 parts (>73,000 parts/yr) and staffing of four workers and one foreman per line.

findings.value: SMC cures 30–150 s, overall cycle as low as 60 s; appropriate above 10,000 parts; steel dies up to 200,000 parts
findings.conditions: glass SMC
findings.source: CW Editorial Team, 'High-volume molding methods', CompositesWorld
findings.quote: Fiberglass thermoset SMC cures in 30 to 150 seconds and overall cycle time can be as low as 60 seconds. ... It is an appropriate choice when production quantities exceed 10,000 parts.

findings.process: compression moulding (SMC, BMC, chopped prepreg SMC-C)
findings.value: cycle ~1–4 min; high volume (100,000 parts per year); 2–30 MPa
findings.conditions: CKN KPC page (draft, rev. 2022-07-26)

findings.quote: Cycle time is around 1 to 4 minutes. ... high volume (100,000 parts per year) ... Typically, the moulding pressure ranges from 2 to 30 MPa (290 to 4350 psi) depending on part shape and complexity.

findings.process: SMC v open mould v RTM (1998)
findings.value: SMC cycle 3–5 min, justified above ~20,000 units/yr; open mould 4–6 h a moulding; RTM 12–90 min
findings.conditions: 1998, glass composites, truck-roof example
